featured_article.title: How MPC and LQR control algorithms keep satellite swarms safe
featured_article.excerpt: When dozens of satellites fly in formation just meters apart, one wrong move could trigger a catastrophic chain reaction of collisions—but Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) algorithms act like an invisible traffic control system in space. These smart algorithms continuously calculate the optimal thrust patterns for each satellite by predicting future positions and minimizing fuel use, while ensuring safe distances are maintained even when unexpected forces like solar radiation pressure try to push the swarm apart. Think of it as giving each satellite a crystal ball that can see several orbits into the future, allowing the entire swarm to dance through space in perfect, fuel-efficient harmony.

topic_highlights.title: NASA Europa Clipper mission to Jupiter's moon
topic_highlights.blurb: NASA's Europa Clipper mission will conduct detailed flybys of Jupiter's ice-covered moon Europa to investigate the vast ocean beneath its frozen surface, which may contain twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined. This groundbreaking mission could reveal whether Europa harbors the conditions necessary for life, potentially answering one of humanity's most profound questions: are we alone in the universe?

topic_highlights.title: Exoskeletons and wearable robots for astronaut ...
topic_highlights.blurb: Exoskeletons and wearable robots could revolutionize spacewalks by counteracting the restrictive forces of pressurized spacesuits, allowing astronauts to move with Earth-like dexterity while performing delicate repairs on spacecraft traveling at 17,500 mph. These powered assistance systems would dramatically extend EVA duration and precision, enabling complex construction tasks essential for building lunar bases, Mars habitats, and deep-space vessels that require intricate assembly in the unforgiving vacuum of space.

topic_highlights.title: J2 perturbation: why orbits drift and how to co...
topic_highlights.blurb: Earth's equatorial bulge creates a gravitational perturbation called J2 that causes satellite orbits to slowly drift and precess over time, making spacecraft gradually deviate from their intended paths. Mission planners must account for this effect when designing long-term satellite constellations like GPS or planning interplanetary trajectories, often requiring periodic orbital corrections to maintain precise positioning for navigation, communication, and scientific observations.
